brief: For each N (<1e12), count the bases b>=2 in which N written in base b has leading digit 1; print INFINITY if there are infinitely many (only when N=1).
key_idea: Leading digit is 1 with k+1 digits iff b^k <= N < 2*b^k, so for each k count b in (floor((N/2)^(1/k)), floor(N^(1/k))].
solution:
1. N=1 -> INFINITY (it is '1' in every base). (N=0 -> 0.)
2. k=1 (two digits): b in (N/2, N] gives N - floor(N/2) bases.
3. For k>=2 while 2^k<=N: add iroot(N,k) - iroot(floor(N/2),k), where iroot(m,k)=largest b with b^k<=m (b^k > N/2 <=> b^k > floor(N/2)).
4. Each base has exactly one digit count, so no double counting; b=1 cancels in the difference.
5. iroot: start from pow(m,1.0/k) and fix up by +-1 with overflow-safe multiplication.
complexity: O(log^2 N) per query (about 40 roots), O(1) space

brief: Golden divisor of n = its largest proper divisor. Players alternately take one of T numbers X and replace it by a smaller positive Y with the same golden divisor; the player with no move loses. Decide the winner.
key_idea: X = d*p with p = smallest prime factor; Y with the same golden divisor d is d*q for prime q<p, so each number is a Nim pile of size (#primes < spf(X)).
solution:
1. Golden divisor of X is X/spf(X). Y has golden divisor d iff Y=d*q with q prime and q<=spf(d); since p<=spf(d), legal moves are exactly q prime, q<p.
2. So a pile with spf p can move to any prime index below it: Grundy(X) = index of spf(X) among primes (2->0, 3->1, 5->2, ...).
3. X=1 has no proper divisor: Grundy 0.
4. Sieve smallest prime factors and prime indices up to max X; XOR all Grundy values.
5. XOR != 0 -> first player wins, else second.
complexity: O(M log log M) sieve with M = max X, O(T) for the game; O(M) space
dry_run:
Own example: X = {9, 4}.
9 = 3*3, spf 3, d=3; can move to 6 only -> Grundy = index(3) = 1.
4 = 2*2, spf 2 -> no smaller prime -> Grundy 0.
XOR = 1 -> First player wins (move 9 -> 6).

brief: Given n integers, find the minimum number of elements whose LCM equals the LCM of the whole array.
key_idea: Each prime of the total LCM needs one chosen element attaining its max exponent: a set cover over the (few) primes, solved by bitmask DP on deduplicated masks.
solution:
1. Factorize every element; for each prime p record the max exponent E[p] (this defines the LCM).
2. Give each prime of the LCM a bit; element mask = primes where its exponent equals E[p].
3. Deduplicate masks (many elements share masks; this is what avoids the TLE).
4. dp[S] = min elements covering prime set S; dp[0]=0; for S increasing, for each mask m: dp[S|m]=min(dp[S|m],dp[S]+1).
5. Answer dp[full]; if the LCM is 1 (all ones) answer 1.
Note: set cover is NP-hard; this relies on the LCM having at most ~20 distinct primes.
complexity: O(n*sqrt(A) factorization + 2^k * (#distinct masks)), k = distinct primes in LCM; O(2^k) space

brief: Array A and M operations: type 1 (L,R): for every i in [L,R], A[i] += F(A[i]) where F = largest power of 2 dividing A[i]; type 2 (L,R): re-execute operations L..R. Print the final array mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Count how many times each op runs (reverse sweep with a difference array over op indices), then how many increments each element gets; x += lowbit(x) turns x into a power of 2 within ~32 steps, after which each step just doubles.
solution:
1. Assume type-2 ranges point to earlier ops. Sweep ops j=M..1 with a running difference sum: cnt[j] = 1 + sum of cnt[t] over type-2 ops t>j covering j.
2. Counts can be exponential: keep each count mod (P-1) for the exponent, plus 'exact small sum' and 'number of big terms' so you know exactly whether it is >= 64 (no saturating subtraction needed).
3. Spread type-1 op counts onto elements with another difference array, giving c_i per element.
4. Per element: simulate x += x & -x up to min(c_i,64) times or until x is a power of 2 (lowbit at least doubles each step, so ~32 steps).
5. Remaining r = c_i - steps: answer = x * 2^r mod P (r taken mod P-1 when c_i is big).
complexity: O(N + M + N*log A + N log P) time, O(N + M) space
dry_run:
Own example: A=[3,5], ops: 1:(1,1,2), 2:(2,1,1).
Reverse sweep: cnt[2]=1, cnt[1]=1+cnt[2]=2.
Element counts c=[2,2].
3 -> 4 (lowbit 1) -> 8; 5 -> 6 -> 8.
Final [8,8].

brief: N soldiers with powers A (each value 1..N/2 appears twice) and bonuses; for each i find the first R>i with A[R] a multiple of A[i] and add max(Bonus[i..R]) (0 if none). Output the total.
key_idea: Sweep right to left keeping the nearest position of each value; for A[i] check all multiples (harmonic sum O(N log N)) and answer the range max with a sparse table.
solution:
1. Build a sparse table on Bonus for O(1) range max.
2. nxt[v] = nearest index > i holding value v (INF initially).
3. For i = N-1 down to 0: R = min over multiples v of A[i] (A[i], 2A[i], ... <= maxV) of nxt[v].
4. If R exists add maxBonus(i, R); then set nxt[A[i]] = i.
5. Each value appears twice, so the total multiple scans are 2*sum(V/v) = O(N log N). Use long long for the sum.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N log N) space
dry_run:
A=[1,1,2,2], Bonus=[4,8,2,1].
i=3 (A=2): nothing to the right -> 0.
i=2 (A=2): R=3 -> max(2,1)=2.
i=1 (A=1): multiples 1,2 -> nearest R=2 -> max(8,2)=8.
i=0 (A=1): R=1 -> max(4,8)=8. Total 18 (matches).

brief: In an N x N matrix, for every cell that is 0, set its whole row and column to 0.
key_idea: First mark which rows and columns contain a zero, then zero them in a second pass (don't zero while scanning).
solution:
1. Pass 1: row[i]=true / col[j]=true for every a[i][j]==0.
2. Pass 2: set a[i][j]=0 if row[i] or col[j].
3. O(1) extra space variant: use first row/column as the markers plus two flags for row 0 / col 0.
4. Edge: zeros created in pass 2 must not trigger more zeroing.

brief: Sum the main and anti-diagonal of a square matrix, counting the centre element only once.
key_idea: Add a[i][i] + a[i][n-1-i] for each i and subtract the centre once if n is odd.
solution:
1. s = sum over i of a[i][i] + a[i][n-1-i].
2. If n is odd, subtract a[n/2][n/2] (it was added twice).
3. Use long long for large values.

brief: m x n matrix: if non-zeros already outnumber zeros print -1; otherwise, in row-major order, replace each zero with the smallest positive v such that max(current row sum, column sum) + v is divisible by 3, stopping once non-zeros outnumber zeros; print the matrix.
key_idea: Straight simulation: recompute row/column sums with the current (already-updated) values before each replacement and stop as soon as nonzero > zero.
solution:
1. Count zeros z and nonzeros nz; if nz > z print -1.
2. Scan row-major; for each zero compute rs (row sum) and cs (column sum) using current values.
3. S = max(rs, cs); v = 3 - S%3 (so S%3==0 gives v=3, smallest positive).
4. Set the cell to v, z--, nz++; stop when nz > z.
5. Caution: a known variant (Q0683 'Sparse Matrix') uses rowsum and divisibility by 2/3 depending on rowsum<=colsum; follow the exact statement given in the exam.
complexity: O(Z*(m+n)) time (Z zeros replaced), O(1) extra space

brief: Find all values that occur 4 times consecutively in a row, column or diagonal of a matrix; print the smallest such value, or -1 if none.
key_idea: From every cell try the 4 directions (right, down, down-right, down-left) and check the next 3 cells; track the minimum matching value.
solution:
1. Directions (0,1),(1,0),(1,1),(1,-1) cover every line once (the other 4 are reverses).
2. For each cell and direction, skip if the 4th cell is out of bounds.
3. If all 4 cells equal, best = min(best, value).
4. Print best or -1. Runs longer than 4 are naturally found too.
dry_run:
Own example (4x4): row 2 = [6,6,6,6], column 0 = [9,9,9,9]? Suppose col 0 is 5,5,5,5 too.
Row run found -> best=6; column run -> best=min(6,5)=5.
Output 5.

brief: Rotate an N x N matrix by 90 degrees (clockwise), ideally in place.
key_idea: Clockwise = transpose then reverse each row; anticlockwise = transpose then reverse each column (or reverse rows first).
solution:
1. Transpose: swap a[i][j] with a[j][i] for j>i.
2. Clockwise: reverse every row.
3. Anticlockwise: instead reverse the order of rows (or each column).
4. Non-square m x n: build a new n x m matrix with b[j][m-1-i]=a[i][j].
dry_run:
Own example: [[1,2],[3,4]].
Transpose -> [[1,3],[2,4]].
Reverse rows -> [[3,1],[4,2]] (clockwise).

brief: Return the elements of an m x n matrix in spiral (clockwise) order.
key_idea: Keep four boundaries top/bottom/left/right and peel one layer at a time, shrinking a boundary after each side.
solution:
1. top=0, bot=m-1, l=0, r=n-1.
2. While top<=bot and l<=r: go right along top (top++), down along r (r--).
3. If top<=bot: go left along bot (bot--).
4. If l<=r: go up along l (l++).
5. The two guards avoid repeating a lone middle row/column.

brief: For each element num1 at (r1,c1) of M1, multiply it by the M2 elements at (r1,r1),(r1,c1),(c1,c1),(c1,r1) that exist; the output at (r1,c1) is the most frequent product (smallest on tie), or -1 if none of those positions exist.
key_idea: Direct simulation: for each cell gather up to 4 products, count with a map, pick max frequency with smallest value.
solution:
1. Output matrix has M1's shape.
2. For (r1,c1) build the 4 positions; keep those with row < rows(M2) and col < cols(M2).
3. Count products num1*M2[r][c] in an ordered map.
4. Iterate the map in increasing key order, keep a product only if its count is strictly greater: this gives the smallest value on ties.
5. No valid position -> -1. (When r1==c1 the 4 positions coincide; they are counted as listed.)

brief: Find the numbers that appear 3 times consecutively in a row, column or diagonal of a matrix; output the minimum such number or -1.
key_idea: Same scan as the 4-in-a-row problem with run length K=3 in 4 directions.
solution:
1. Check the 4 directions (0,1),(1,0),(1,1),(1,-1) from every cell; the other 4 are reverses.
2. Skip if the last cell of the run would be out of bounds.
3. If all K cells are equal, best = min(best, value).
4. Print best, or -1 if no run was found (longer runs are found automatically).

3. If all K cells are equal, best = min(best, value).

brief: Print every 2x2 submatrix of an integer matrix in which each of the four elements is divisible by the sum of its own digits.
key_idea: Precompute ok[i][j] = (a[i][j] % digitSum(a[i][j]) == 0), then check each 2x2 window.
solution:
1. digitSum on |v|; treat 0 (digit sum 0) as not divisible.
2. ok[i][j] per cell (each cell computed once).
3. For every top-left (i,j) with i<m-1, j<n-1: if all four ok, print the 2x2 block.
4. Print in row-major order of the top-left corner; print -1/nothing if none (follow the statement).

key_idea: Length-4 equal-run scan in 4 directions; the min over all found values covers both the 'one set' and 'many sets' cases.
solution:
1. Check the 4 directions (0,1),(1,0),(1,1),(1,-1) from every cell; the other 4 are reverses.
2. Skip if the last cell of the run would be out of bounds.
3. If all K cells are equal, best = min(best, value).

brief: An m x n matrix is sparse if #zeros >= #nonzeros (else print -1). Replace zeros in row-major order: if rowsum <= colsum use the smallest positive num making rowsum+num divisible by 2, else divisible by 3; stop once nonzeros outnumber zeros, then print.
key_idea: Simulate with live row/column sums; the sample shows replacement stops as soon as nonzeros > zeros.
solution:
1. Count zeros z, nonzeros nz; if z < nz print -1.
2. Row-major scan; for each zero (while nz <= z) compute current rs and cs.
3. If rs <= cs: num = (rs%2==0) ? 2 : 1; else num = 3 - rs%3 (gives 3 when rs%3==0).
4. Set the cell, z--, nz++.
5. Print the matrix. (Sample confirms rowsum is used in the <= branch; the 'divisible by 3' branch is assumed to also use rowsum.)

brief: Binary grid: find the minimum number of cells to change so that every right/down path from top-left to bottom-right reads as a palindrome.
key_idea: Cells with i+j=d sit at step d on every path; layer d must equal layer (n+m-2-d), so all cells in the two layers must be one value -> cost min(#0,#1).
solution:
1. L = n+m-2 (last step). Count cnt[d][v] for every cell with d=i+j.
2. For d < L-d: cells of layers d and L-d must all be equal; cost += min(total zeros, total ones) in both layers.
3. If L is even, the middle layer d=L/2 is free (it pairs with itself).
4. Sum the costs.

Layer 0 {1}, layer 2 {1}: zeros 0, ones 2 -> cost 0.
Layer 1 {1,0} is the middle -> free. Answer 0.

brief: Given an N x M grid of letters, find the minimum number of cells to replace so that every right/down path from (1,1) to (N,M) reads as a palindrome.
key_idea: Anti-diagonal layers d and N+M-2-d must all hold one letter; cost = cells in both layers minus the most frequent letter there.
solution:
1. L = N+M-2; cnt[d][c] = how many cells with i+j=d hold letter c.
2. For each pair d < L-d: total = sum of both layers, best = max over c of cnt[d][c]+cnt[L-d][c]; add total - best.
3. The middle layer (L even) needs no change.
4. N,M<=1e3 -> 1e6 cells, 26 letters per layer: fast.

Layer 1 {c,b} is the middle -> free.
Answer 1 (matches).

brief: Given a binary matrix (rows of comma-separated 0/1), output the area of the largest sub-matrix of all 1s; if that area is 1 or less, output -1.
key_idea: Treat each row as the base of a histogram of consecutive 1s above it and take the largest rectangle in histogram with a monotonic stack.
solution:
1. Parse each line, splitting on commas.
2. h[j] = h[j]+1 if cell is 1 else 0, row by row.
3. For each row, largest rectangle in histogram: stack of increasing heights; on pop, width = i - stack.top() - 1.
4. Track the max area; print -1 if max <= 1.
5. If the paper means a square sub-matrix, use dp[i][j]=min(up,left,diag)+1 and area=side^2 instead (both give 9 for a 3x3 block).

brief: Write a recursive Fibonacci function and analyse its time and space complexity.
key_idea: fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2) recomputes subproblems: time O(phi^n) ~ O(2^n), stack depth O(n); memoization makes it O(n).
solution:
1. Base: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1.
2. Recurse fib(n-1)+fib(n-2).
3. Time: the call tree has about fib(n) leaves -> O(1.618^n) (often stated O(2^n)).
4. Space: O(n) for the recursion stack (deepest chain n, n-1, ..., 1).
5. Improvement: memo array -> O(n) time; iterative two variables -> O(1) space; matrix power -> O(log n).
complexity: Naive: O(2^n) time, O(n) stack; memoized: O(n) time, O(n) space

fib(3) = fib(2)+fib(1) = (1+0)+1 = 2
fib(2) = 1 (computed twice -> the waste)

brief: Write a recursive function to compute n! (factorial).
key_idea: fact(n) = n * fact(n-1) with base fact(0)=fact(1)=1.
solution:
1. Base case: n<=1 returns 1.
2. Otherwise return n * fact(n-1).
3. Use long long (fits up to 20!); for larger n use mod or big integers.
4. Negative input: reject / undefined.

brief: Write Fibonacci with recursion, then optimize it.
key_idea: Naive recursion is exponential; memoization (top-down) or bottom-up iteration makes it linear, and O(1) space with two variables.
solution:
1. Naive: fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2), base 0->0, 1->1; O(2^n).
2. Memoize results in an array: each n computed once -> O(n).
3. Bottom-up: a=0,b=1; repeat n times (a,b)=(b,a+b) -> O(n) time O(1) space.
4. For huge n with mod: matrix exponentiation / fast doubling in O(log n).

brief: Reverse the digits of an integer using a recursive function.
key_idea: Carry the partially built reverse as an accumulator: rev(n, acc) = rev(n/10, acc*10 + n%10).
solution:
1. Base: n==0 -> return acc.
2. Recurse with n/10 and acc*10 + n%10.
3. Handle negatives by reversing |n| and restoring the sign.
4. Trailing zeros vanish (1200 -> 21); use long long to avoid overflow.
complexity: O(d) time, O(d) stack space (d = number of digits)

brief: Generate all subsequences of a string, e.g. 'abc'.
key_idea: At each index either include or exclude the character: 2^n leaves of a binary recursion tree.
solution:
1. solve(i, cur): if i==n output cur (including the empty string if required).
2. Include: solve(i+1, cur + s[i]).
3. Exclude: solve(i+1, cur).
4. Alternative: iterate masks 0..2^n-1 and take the set bits.
5. For unique subsequences with repeated letters, put them in a set.

brief: Print the sequence of moves that solves Tower of Hanoi for N disks.
key_idea: Move N-1 disks to the helper peg, move the largest disk, then move the N-1 disks on top of it: 2^N - 1 moves.
solution:
1. hanoi(n, from, to, via): if n==0 return.
2. hanoi(n-1, from, via, to).
3. Print 'move disk n from -> to'.
4. hanoi(n-1, via, to, from).
5. Moves T(n)=2T(n-1)+1 = 2^n - 1.

brief: Return all permutations of an array or string.
key_idea: Fix each unused element at the current position, recurse, then undo (used[] marking or in-place swaps).
solution:
1. rec(i): if i==n record the current arrangement.
2. For j from i to n-1: swap(a[i],a[j]), rec(i+1), swap back.
3. Equivalent: build a path with a used[] array.
4. Duplicates: sort and use next_permutation, or skip a value already tried at this level.
5. n! results, so only feasible for n <= ~10.
complexity: O(n * n!) time, O(n) recursion depth

solution:

2. Include the empty subset unless the statement says otherwise.
3. If the array has duplicates and unique subsets are wanted: sort, then in recursion skip a[i]==a[i-1] at the same depth.
4. Since the samples were contradictory, check the expected order (lexicographic vs mask order) and whether [] is printed.

brief: Generate all permutations of a string using swap-based recursion (explain on paper).
key_idea: Position i takes each of s[i..n-1] in turn via swap, recurse on i+1, swap back to restore.
solution:
1. permute(s, i): if i==n print s.
2. For j=i..n-1: swap(s[i],s[j]); permute(s,i+1); swap(s[i],s[j]).
3. The second swap (backtrack) is what keeps the string correct for the next j.
4. For repeated characters, keep a seen-set per level to avoid duplicate outputs.
dry_run: 'abc', i=0: j=0 'abc' -> (i=1) abc, acb; j=1 swap -> 'bac' -> bac, bca; j=2 swap -> 'cba' -> cba, cab.

brief: Print all permutations of the characters of a given string.
key_idea: Sort the string then loop next_permutation (gives unique permutations in lexicographic order), or use swap-based recursion.
solution:
1. sort(s).
2. do { print s; } while(next_permutation(s)).
3. This handles repeated characters (no duplicates) and gives sorted order.
4. Recursive alternative: swap-based permute(s, i).
complexity: O(n * n!) time, O(1) extra space
dry_run: s='bac' -> sorted 'abc': abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba (next_permutation returns false after cba).

brief: Reverse a stack using only recursion (no extra container).
key_idea: Pop everything recursively, and on the way back insert each element at the bottom (insertAtBottom is itself recursive).
solution:
1. reverse(st): if empty return; x=top, pop; reverse(st); insertAtBottom(st,x).
2. insertAtBottom(st,x): if empty push x; else y=top, pop, insertAtBottom(st,x), push y.
3. The call stack acts as temporary storage.
dry_run:
Stack bottom->top [1,2,3]:
pop 3, pop 2, pop 1 -> empty.
insertAtBottom 1 -> [1]; insert 2 at bottom -> [2,1]; insert 3 -> [3,2,1].

brief: Generate all permutations of a string or array.
key_idea: Backtracking: choose an unused element for each position (used[] array), recurse, unchoose.
solution:
1. path empty, used[] all false.
2. If path size == n, record it.
3. For each i not used: mark, push a[i], recurse, pop, unmark.
4. For duplicates: sort, and skip i if a[i]==a[i-1] and !used[i-1].
complexity: O(n * n!) time, O(n) space besides output

brief: Generate valid (distinct) permutations with recursion/backtracking using swaps, explained on paper.
key_idea: Swap-based permutation, but at each depth swap in each distinct character only once so repeated characters don't produce duplicates.
solution:
1. permute(s, i): if i==n record s.
2. Keep a local set 'tried' for this depth.
3. For j=i..n-1: if s[j] already tried skip; else add, swap(s[i],s[j]), recurse i+1, swap back.
4. 'Valid' is interpreted as distinct permutations; if the exam adds a constraint (e.g. no two equal adjacent), check it before recording or prune early.
complexity: O(n * n!) worst-case time, O(n^2) space for per-level sets
dry_run:
'aab': i=0 tries 'a' (j=0) -> aab, aba; skips j=1 ('a' tried); tries 'b' -> baa.
3 distinct permutations.

brief: Generate all balanced parentheses strings with n pairs.
key_idea: Add '(' while open < n, add ')' while close < open; every completed string of length 2n is valid.
solution:
1. rec(cur, open, close): if cur length == 2n record.
2. If open < n: rec(cur+'(', open+1, close).
3. If close < open: rec(cur+')', open, close+1).
4. Count of results = Catalan(n).

brief: Split a list of integers into two non-empty groups whose sizes differ by at most one, minimizing the absolute difference of their sums.
key_idea: One group has exactly floor(n/2) elements; compute which sums are reachable with exactly k elements (count-constrained subset-sum) and pick the sum closest to total/2.
solution:
1. k = n/2 (the other group has n-k, so sizes differ by <= 1); n>=2.
2. dp[c][s] = can choose c elements with sum s; dp[0][0]=true.
3. For each element x, for c from k down to 1, for s from S down to x: dp[c][s] |= dp[c-1][s-x].
4. Answer = min over s with dp[k][s] of |S - 2s|.
5. Assumes non-negative values (shift values if negatives appear); for tiny n the include/exclude recursion with a size counter is fine too.
complexity: O(n * k * S) time, O(k * S) space (S = total sum)
dry_run:
Own example: [3,1,4,2]: S=10, k=2.
Pairs reachable with 2 elements: 4,7,5,5,3,6.
Closest to 5: s=5 -> |10-10|=0 (e.g. {3,2} vs {1,4}).
Answer 0.

brief: Given an array and a target K, find and return a subset whose elements sum to K (empty / -1 if none).
key_idea: Subset-sum DP table dp[i][s] = can the first i elements make s; walk back from dp[n][K] to recover the chosen elements.
solution:
1. dp[0][0]=true; dp[i][s] = dp[i-1][s] || (s>=a[i-1] && dp[i-1][s-a[i-1]]).
2. If dp[n][K] is false, no subset exists.
3. Reconstruct: for i=n..1, if dp[i-1][s] is false the element a[i-1] must be taken: add it and s -= a[i-1].
4. Small n alternative (as in the interview): recursion pick/skip returning on the first success.
5. Assumes non-negative integers.

brief: A recursion/backtracking problem that explores all combinations to find required results (LeetCode-medium level); exact statement not given.
key_idea: Statement unknown; the generic template is choose / explore / unchoose with pruning.
solution:
1. Too vague to solve: the actual combination problem is not specified.
2. Generic template: rec(start, path): if goal reached record; for i in [start,n): choose a[i], rec(i+1 or i), unchoose.
3. Prune branches that can't reach the goal (e.g. sum already exceeds target after sorting).
4. Practise Combination Sum, Subsets, Permutations, N-Queens to cover this pattern.
dry_run: Own example: not possible without the statement.

brief: Given distinct candidates and a target, return all unique combinations summing to target where each candidate may be reused any number of times.
key_idea: Backtrack with a start index (stay on i to allow reuse, never go back to avoid permutations of the same combo); sort to prune.
solution:
1. Sort candidates.
2. rec(start, remaining, path): if remaining==0 record path.
3. For i from start: if c[i] > remaining break (sorted pruning).
4. Push c[i], rec(i, remaining-c[i]) (i, not i+1, allows reuse), pop.
complexity: Exponential: O(N^(T/min+1)) worst case; O(T/min) depth
dry_run:
[2,3,6,7], 7:
2,2,2 -> rem 1 -> 2 too big -> back; 2,2,3 -> rem 0 -> record.
2,3,... rem 2 -> 3 too big; 3,3 -> rem 1 dead; 6 -> rem 1 dead; 7 -> record.
Result [[2,2,3],[7]] (matches).

brief: Place N queens on an N x N board so that no two attack each other; count and/or list all solutions.
key_idea: Place one queen per row; track used columns and both diagonals (r+c and r-c) so each check is O(1); bitmasks make it very fast.
solution:
1. rec(row): if row==N record the board.
2. For each col: if col, (row+col), (row-col+N-1) all free, place the queen, mark, rec(row+1), unmark.
3. Bitmask version: avail = ~(cols|d1|d2) & full; take lowest bit p; recurse with (cols|p, (d1|p)<<1, (d2|p)>>1).
4. N=1 -> 1 solution, N=2,3 -> 0.
complexity: O(N!) time worst case, O(N) space
dry_run:
N=4: row0 col1 -> row1 col3 -> row2 col0 -> row3 col2 -> solution .Q.. / ...Q / Q... / ..Q.
Other solution mirrors it: col2,0,3,1. Count = 2.

brief: Solve a 9x9 Sudoku: fill empty cells so every row, column and 3x3 box contains digits 1-9 exactly once.
key_idea: Backtracking over empty cells with row/column/box bitmasks for O(1) validity checks.
solution:
1. Masks row[r], col[c], box[(r/3)*3+c/3] of used digits; collect empty cells.
2. rec(k): if k == #empty return true.
3. For cell (r,c), try each digit d not in row|col|box masks: set, recurse; if success return true; else undo.
4. Return false if no digit works (backtrack).
5. Speed-up: pick the empty cell with fewest candidates first (MRV).
complexity: Exponential worst case (9^E), fast in practice; O(81) space
dry_run:
Own example: a cell whose row has {1..8} used except 9 and col/box allow 9 -> only candidate 9, placed directly.
A cell with candidates {2,5}: try 2, deeper cell has no candidate -> undo, try 5 -> continues.

brief: Convert a 3x3 matrix into a 'Smart Matrix' (distinct 1..9, every row, column and both diagonal sums divisible by 5) at minimum conversion cost.
key_idea: Only 9! = 362880 arrangements exist (128 are valid); precompute the valid ones and take the one with minimum cost to the input.
solution:
1. Enumerate permutations of 1..9 with next_permutation; keep those whose 3 rows, 3 columns and 2 diagonals have sum % 5 == 0 (128 squares).
2. Cost assumed = sum over cells of |input - target| (like the magic-square problem; adjust if the exam defines cost differently).
3. Answer = min cost over the valid squares.
4. Precompute once; each test is then 128*9 operations.
complexity: O(9! * 9) precompute, O(128*9) per query; O(128*9) space

brief: Print the top 7 employees by salary, and rename a column of a table.
key_idea: ORDER BY salary DESC with LIMIT 7 (or DENSE_RANK if ties at the cut must be included); ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN.
complexity: O(n log n) for the sort (O(n log 7) with a top-N heap)
dry_run:
Own example: salaries 90,80,80,70,60,50,40,30.
LIMIT 7 -> first seven rows 90..40.
DENSE_RANK<=7 also returns 30 (ranks 1,2,2,3,4,5,6,7).

brief: Retrieve the name of the employee with the maximum salary.
key_idea: Compare salary with a scalar subquery MAX(salary) so all tied top earners are returned.
complexity: O(n) (two scans) or O(n log n) with ORDER BY
dry_run:
Own example: (A,50),(B,70),(C,70).
MAX = 70 -> returns B and C.

brief: Compute monthly salary from a yearly salary column, and find the second-highest salary.
key_idea: Monthly = annual/12 in the SELECT list; second highest = MAX of salaries strictly below the MAX.
solution:
1. SELECT name, salary/12.0 AS monthly_salary FROM Employee;  (use ROUND(salary/12.0,2) if needed; /12.0 avoids integer division)
2. SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);
3. Returns NULL if there is no second distinct salary.
4. Window alternative: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 2.
dry_run:
Own example: salaries 120000, 96000, 120000.
Monthly -> 10000, 8000, 10000.
MAX=120000; MAX below it = 96000.

brief: Write a query to find duplicate rows in a table.
key_idea: GROUP BY all columns that define a duplicate and keep groups with COUNT(*) > 1.
dry_run:
Own example: rows (1,a@x),(2,b@x),(3,a@x) on email.
Group a@x count 2 -> reported; b@x count 1 -> not.

brief: Find the third highest salary from the employee table.
key_idea: Rank distinct salaries: LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2 over DISTINCT salaries, or DENSE_RANK = 3.
dry_run:
Own example: 100,90,90,80,70.
Distinct desc: 100,90,80,70 -> offset 2 -> 80.

brief: Given Employee(EmployeeID, Name, Department), display the number of employees in each department.
key_idea: GROUP BY Department with COUNT(*).
complexity: O(n log n) (or O(n) hash aggregate)
dry_run:
Own example: (1,A,IT),(2,B,HR),(3,C,IT).
IT -> 2, HR -> 1.

brief: List employee details whose salary is more than the average salary.
key_idea: Compare each salary against a scalar subquery AVG(salary).
dry_run:
Own example: salaries 30,50,70 -> AVG 50.
Only the 70 employee is returned (50 is not strictly greater).

brief: Write a SQL query to find the 5th highest salary in a table.
key_idea: DISTINCT salaries ordered descending with OFFSET 4, or DENSE_RANK = 5, or the correlated-count method.
complexity: O(n log n) (O(n^2) for the correlated version)
dry_run:
Own example: 100,90,80,80,70,60.
Distinct desc 100,90,80,70,60 -> 5th = 60.
Correlated: for 60, distinct salaries above = 4 -> match.

brief: Write a SQL query to find the second smallest salary in a table.
key_idea: MIN of salaries strictly greater than the overall MIN (or ascending DISTINCT with OFFSET 1).
dry_run:
Own example: 40,20,20,30.
MIN=20; MIN of salaries > 20 = 30.

brief: SQL query for the second-largest salary in an employee table.
key_idea: MAX of salaries strictly below the overall MAX; handles duplicates of the top value.
dry_run:
Own example: 300,300,200,100.
MAX=300; MAX below 300 = 200.

brief: Write SQL to find and remove duplicate rows from a table (keep one copy).
key_idea: Find duplicates with GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*)>1; delete all but the smallest id per duplicate group (self-join or ROW_NUMBER).
dry_run:
Own example: (1,a),(2,b),(3,a),(4,a).
Group a has ids 1,3,4 -> keep MIN 1, delete 3 and 4.
Result (1,a),(2,b).

brief: Write a SQL query to get the maximum and the second maximum salary.
key_idea: Two scalar subqueries in one SELECT: MAX, and MAX below MAX.
dry_run:
Own example: 500,400,400,300.
max_salary = 500, second_max = 400.

brief: Find employees belonging to more than 5 departments, using IN instead of a top-level GROUP BY.
key_idea: Filter with IN over the set of empIDs whose department count exceeds 5; a correlated COUNT avoids GROUP BY entirely.
complexity: O(n log n) for version 1, O(n^2) worst case for the correlated version
dry_run:
Own example: emp 7 appears with depts 1..6, emp 8 with depts 1..2.
Inner set = {7} -> rows of emp 7 returned; emp 8 excluded.

brief: Remove duplicate rows from a table, and find the nth highest salary.
key_idea: Delete all but MIN(id) per duplicate group; nth highest = DISTINCT salaries with OFFSET n-1 or DENSE_RANK = n.
dry_run:
Own example: salaries 100,100,90,80, N=2.
Distinct desc 100,90,80 -> OFFSET 1 -> 90.
Duplicate rows (1,x),(2,x) -> id 2 deleted.

brief: LeetCode 1934 Confirmation Rate: for each user in Signups, the fraction of their Confirmations rows with action 'confirmed' (0 if none), rounded to 2 decimals.
key_idea: LEFT JOIN Signups to Confirmations so users without messages stay, then AVG of a 1/0 CASE, with IFNULL/COALESCE to 0.
solution:
1. SELECT s.user_id, ROUND(IFNULL(AVG(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END), 0), 2) AS confirmation_rate
   FROM Signups s LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id GROUP BY s.user_id;
2. Note: with no matching rows c.action is NULL, so the CASE gives 0 and AVG = 0 anyway; IFNULL is a safety net.
3. Alternative: ROUND(SUM(c.action='confirmed') / COUNT(*), 2) in MySQL.
complexity: O(n + m) with hashing / O((n+m) log) with sort
dry_run:
Own example: user 3 has confirmed, timeout; user 6 has none; user 7 has 3 confirmed.
User 3: (1+0)/2 = 0.50; user 6: LEFT JOIN row with NULL -> 0.00; user 7: 1.00.

brief: From EMP(empID, firstName, lastName, deptID), find employees who are in more than 5 departments using an IN clause instead of grouping in the main query.
key_idea: Outer query filters with empID IN (subquery of employees having > 5 distinct deptIDs); a correlated count removes GROUP BY completely.
dry_run:
Own example: emp 1 in depts {10,20,30,40,50,60}, emp 2 in {10}.
Subquery -> {1}; output emp 1 once.

brief: Tables products(productId, deptId, price) and transactions(productId, deptId, transactionDate, price, status): count successful transactions per day per department.
key_idea: Filter status = 'success', GROUP BY the calendar date and deptId.
solution:
1. SELECT DATE(t.transactionDate) AS txn_day, t.deptId, COUNT(*) AS successful_txns
   FROM transactions t WHERE t.status = 'success'
   GROUP BY DATE(t.transactionDate), t.deptId ORDER BY txn_day, t.deptId;
2. DATE() strips the time part (SQL Server: CAST(transactionDate AS DATE)).
3. If the department must come from products: JOIN products p ON p.productId = t.productId and group by p.deptId.
4. Check the exact status literal ('SUCCESS', 'successful', ...).

brief: Find the highest-paid employee in each department using RANK()/PARTITION BY; also get the current HOD of each department from historical records.
key_idea: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1; current HOD = latest record per department (ROW_NUMBER by start_date DESC, or end_date IS NULL).
solution:
1. SELECT dept_id, emp_id, name, salary FROM (SELECT e.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) rk FROM Employee e) t WHERE rk = 1;  (RANK keeps ties)
2. Assumed history table HOD_History(dept_id, emp_id, start_date, end_date).
3. SELECT dept_id, emp_id FROM (SELECT h.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY start_date DESC) rn FROM HOD_History h) x WHERE rn = 1;
4. Or simply WHERE end_date IS NULL if the open record marks the current HOD.
dry_run:
Own example: IT: (A,90),(B,90),(C,50) -> rk 1,1,3 -> A and B.
HOD_History IT: (X,2019),(Y,2023) -> rn 1 = Y is current HOD.

brief: Using car manufacturer, customer and car (sale) tables, find customers who bought a red car from a given manufacturer and live in a given area.
key_idea: Join customer -> car -> manufacturer and filter colour, manufacturer name and area (or nest IN subqueries).
complexity: O(n log n) with indexed joins
dry_run:
Own example: Car rows (c1,Tata,Red,cust1), (c2,Tata,Blue,cust2), (c3,Ford,Red,cust3); cust1 area Pune.
Only cust1 passes all three filters.

brief: Find employees having the top-K salaries in each department without using LIMIT.
key_idea: DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) <= K; or a correlated count of distinct higher salaries in the same department < K.
dry_run:
Own example K=2, dept IT salaries 90,80,80,70.
DENSE_RANK 1,2,2,3 -> 90,80,80 returned.
Correlated: for 70, distinct higher = {90,80} = 2, not < 2 -> excluded.

brief: Table (user_id, login_data timestamp): find the user with the longest streak of consecutive login days (latest streak wins ties).
key_idea: Gaps-and-islands: on distinct login dates, date minus ROW_NUMBER is constant within a run of consecutive days.
solution:
1. WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(login_data) AS day FROM Logins),
2. g AS (SELECT user_id, day, DATE_SUB(day, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) DAY) AS grp FROM d),
3. s AS (SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS streak, MAX(day) AS streak_end FROM g GROUP BY user_id, grp)
4. SELECT user_id, streak FROM s ORDER BY streak DESC, streak_end DESC LIMIT 1;
5. DISTINCT dates first so several logins on one day don't break the run; Postgres: day - ROW_NUMBER()::int; SQL Server: DATEADD(day, -rn, day).
dry_run:
Own example: user 1 days 1,2,3,5; user 2 days 4,5.
User 1: rn 1,2,3,4 -> grp 0,0,0,1 -> streaks 3 and 1.
User 2: grp 3,3 -> streak 2. Answer user 1 with 3.

brief: Support range updates (add v to A[l..r]) and range-sum queries efficiently.
key_idea: Two Fenwick trees: prefix(i) = sum(B1,i)*i - sum(B2,i) handles range add + range sum in O(log n) (or a lazy segment tree).
solution:
1. add(l,r,v): B1 += v at l, -v at r+1; B2 += v*(l-1) at l, -v*r at r+1.
2. prefix(i) = query(B1,i)*i - query(B2,i).
3. sum(l,r) = prefix(r) - prefix(l-1).
4. Initial array: add(i,i,A[i]) for each i (or keep a separate static prefix-sum array).
5. Use long long; offline-only updates then queries -> a plain difference array is enough.
complexity: O((n+q) log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Array A of size N and M queries (X,Y): decrease A[X-1] by Y (persistently), then build prefix-min array B and report the number of distinct values in B after each query.
key_idea: Distinct values of B = number of strict prefix-minimum 'records'; keep records in an ordered map and, since values only decrease, each update inserts at most one record and deletes the later ones it dominates.
solution:
1. Records = positions i with A[i] < min(A[0..i-1]); their values strictly decrease; answer = #records.
2. Store records in map<pos,val>.
3. Update p=X-1: A[p]-=Y, v=A[p]; prevMin = value of the last record before p (INF if none).
4. If v >= prevMin nothing changes (p wasn't and isn't a record). Else set rec[p]=v and erase following records with value >= v.
5. Each query inserts <= 1 record, so total erasures <= N+M: amortized O(log N).
complexity: O((N+M) log N) time, O(N) space

brief: Given a permutation of 1..N and K, you may reverse at most one contiguous subarray of length K; return the minimum possible number of inversions.
key_idea: Reversing a window only flips pairs inside it: new total = total + C(K,2) - 2*inv(window); slide the window with a BIT to find the window with max inversions.
solution:
1. total = inversions of the whole array (BIT over values).
2. Pairs with one element outside keep their relative order, so only inside pairs change: inside inv becomes C(K,2) - inv(W).
3. Sliding window with a BIT of the window's values: removing leftmost x subtracts #smaller in window; adding y adds #greater in window.
4. best = max inv(W); answer = min(total, total + K(K-1)/2 - 2*best) ('at most one').
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space

brief: The hardest of 3 SP OA questions, solvable with a segment tree (about CF 1700-1800); the statement was not recalled.
key_idea: Statement unknown; only that it needed a segment tree.
solution:
1. Too vague to solve: no statement, constraints or sample.
2. Prepare the standard toolkit: point update/range query, lazy propagation (range add/assign + range sum/min), segment tree with custom merge nodes (e.g. longest run), and BIT for counting.
3. See Q0738, Q0739 and Q0734 in this set for typical Infosys segment-tree tasks.
dry_run: Own example: not possible without the statement.

brief: Number X with N digits and Q queries: (1,L,R) sets digit L to R; (2,L,R) asks the longest subsegment of X[L..R] with no two adjacent equal digits. Output the product of all type-2 answers (1 if none).
key_idea: Segment tree node keeps (len, prefix run, suffix run, best, first digit, last digit); two halves join across the middle iff left.last != right.first.
solution:
1. Leaf: len=pre=suf=best=1, first=last=digit.
2. Merge a,b: ok = a.last != b.first; pre = a.pre==a.len && ok ? a.len+b.pre : a.pre; suf symmetric; best = max(a.best, b.best, ok ? a.suf+b.pre : 0).
3. Type 1: point update; type 2: range query combining nodes in order.
4. Multiply answers; modulus is not stated, 1e9+7 assumed.
5. Read X as a string (N can exceed 18 digits).
complexity: O((N + Q) log N) time, O(N) space

brief: Process q queries on A: type 1 (l,r) sets A[i]=(i-l+1)*A[l] for l<=i<=r; type 2 (l,r) asks the sum of A[l..r]. Output the sum of all type-2 answers mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: (i-l+1)*c = c*i + c*(1-l) is a linear function of the index, so use a lazy segment tree whose tag assigns A[i] = a*i + b; a node's sum = a*(sum of indices) + b*len.
solution:
1. Build a sum segment tree mod P on A (1-based).
2. Type 1: c = point query A[l]; then range-assign tag (a=c, b=c*(1-l) mod P) on [l,r].
3. Applying tag to [L,R]: sum = a*(L+...+R) + b*(R-L+1) mod P; push tags down before recursing (assignment overrides older tags).
4. Type 2: range sum; accumulate into the answer mod P.
5. Values grow multiplicatively, so keep everything mod P (the operations are linear, so mod is safe).
complexity: O((n + q) log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example: A=[2,5,7]; query (1,1,3): c=2 -> A=[2,4,6] (a=2, b=0).
Query (2,2,3) -> 4+6 = 10.
Total of type-2 answers = 10.

brief: Count pairs i<j where freq of A[i] in A[1..i] + freq of A[j] in A[j..N] <= floor(distinct(1..i)/2) + floor(distinct(j..N)/2); answer mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Separate i-terms and j-terms: X_i = f_i - floor(dp_i/2) <= Y_j = floor(ds_j/2) - g_j, then count with a BIT while sweeping j.
solution:
1. Let f_i = freq of A[i] in A[1..i], dp_i = distinct(1..i); g_j = freq of A[j] in A[j..N], ds_j = distinct(j..N).
2. Condition f_i + g_j <= dp_i/2 + ds_j/2 rearranges to X_i <= Y_j with X_i = f_i - floor(dp_i/2), Y_j = floor(ds_j/2) - g_j.
3. Compute X left to right and Y right to left with hash maps.
4. Sweep j=2..N: insert X_{j-1} into a BIT (offset by N+1 for negatives), add count of inserted X <= Y_j.
5. Output the count mod 1e9+7.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space

brief: For each query subtract x from A[L-1] (changes persist); B is the prefix-min array of A; report the number of distinct values in B after each query.
key_idea: Distinct prefix minima = number of strict new-minimum positions; maintain them in an ordered map under point decreases (amortized deletions).
solution:
1. Records: positions where A[i] < every earlier value; answer = #records.
2. map<pos,val>; for update at p: v = A[p] - x; prevMin = last record value before p.
3. If v < prevMin: rec[p]=v and delete following records with value >= v; else nothing changes.
4. Output map size after each query.
5. Assumes x >= 0 (a pure decrease); for increases the structure would need a segment tree instead.
complexity: O((N+Q) log N) time, O(N) space
dry_run:
Own example: A=[4,6,2], records {0:4,2:2} -> 2.
Query L=2, x=3: A[1]=3 < 4 -> add {1:3}; next record 2 < 3 stays -> 3 (B=[4,3,2]).

brief: Count pairs i<j with frequency(1,i,A[i]) + frequency(j,N,A[j]) <= floor(distinct(1,i)/2) + floor(distinct(j,N)/2), mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Rewrite as X_i <= Y_j with X_i = f_i - floor(dp_i/2), Y_j = floor(ds_j/2) - g_j and count with a Fenwick tree.
solution:
1. Let f_i = freq of A[i] in A[1..i], dp_i = distinct(1..i); g_j = freq of A[j] in A[j..N], ds_j = distinct(j..N).
2. Condition f_i + g_j <= dp_i/2 + ds_j/2 rearranges to X_i <= Y_j with X_i = f_i - floor(dp_i/2), Y_j = floor(ds_j/2) - g_j.
3. Compute X left to right and Y right to left with hash maps.
4. Sweep j=2..N: insert X_{j-1} into a BIT (offset by N+1 for negatives), add count of inserted X <= Y_j.
5. Output the count mod 1e9+7.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space

brief: N trees with heights A[i] and growth B[i] per unit of fertilizer; over M days, type-1 ops add K fertilizer to trees L..R, type-2 ops check one tree and cut it if its height exceeds K. Return the sum of heights after M days mod 1e9+7 (statement garbled).
key_idea: Height of tree i = base_i + B[i]*(fertilizer received since last cut); range fertilizer adds can be tracked with a BIT of range adds and point queries, and a cut resets the base.
solution:
1. Statement is garbled: what a 'cut' leaves (0? K?) and whether growth is per day is unclear, so this is only a sketch.
2. BIT over trees for range-add of fertilizer, point query F(i).
3. For each tree store base[i] and the F value at its last cut, off[i]; height = base[i] + B[i]*(F(i) - off[i]).
4. Type 2: compute height; if > K, cut (set base to the cut height, off[i]=F(i)).
5. At the end sum all heights mod 1e9+7.
complexity: O((N + M) log N) time, O(N) space (under the assumed reading)
dry_run:
Own example (assumed: cut sets height to 0): A=[1,2], B=[1,3]; add K=2 to [1,2] -> heights 3, 8.
Query tree 2 with K=5: 8 > 5 -> cut to 0.
Sum = 3 + 0 = 3.

brief: Given a permutation p of length n and k, delete exactly one contiguous subarray of length k; the cost is the number of inversions of the remaining sequence. Output the minimum cost mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Inversions removed by deleting window W = sum over W of c(x) - inv(W), where c(x) = #greater before x + #smaller after x (inside pairs are counted twice in the sum).
solution:
1. total = all inversions; c[i] = greater-before + smaller-after (two BIT passes).
2. Deleting W removes every inversion touching W: sum c(W) counts cross pairs once and inside pairs twice, so removed = sumC(W) - inv(W).
3. Slide the window: sumC by add/subtract, inv(W) with a BIT of window values (drop leftmost: minus #smaller; add right: plus #greater).
4. answer = total - max removed, then mod 1e9+7. k=n gives 0.
5. Source text says 'almost k'; this assumes exactly k.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Own example: p=[3,1,2], k=1. total = 2; c = [2,1,1].
Windows: delete 3 -> 2-0 = 2 removed; delete 1 -> 1; delete 2 -> 1.
Answer 2-2 = 0 (remaining [1,2]).

brief: Queries: type 1 (l,r) sets A[i]=(i-l+1)*A[l] for i in [l,r]; type 2 returns the sum of A[l..r]; output the sum of type-2 answers mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Assignment of an arithmetic progression = assigning the linear function c*i + c*(1-l); lazy segment tree with (a,b) tags and index-sum formula.
solution:
1. Segment tree of sums mod P with lazy tag 'A[i] = a*i + b' (assignment).
2. Type 1: c = A[l] (point query, done before the update), then assign (a=c, b=c*(1-l)) on [l,r].
3. Node [L,R] sum under tag = a*(L+R)*(R-L+1)/2 + b*(R-L+1) (mod P, use inverse of 2).
4. Type 2: range sum, add to running total mod P.
5. Note tag assignment overwrites children's older tags on push.
complexity: O((n + q) log n) time, O(n) space
